Introduction:
When we look out upon the creatures of the earth and what comes to them, we see that Hashem gave mankind a great share in the settling of this world and in completing all that fills it, so much so that we may say that the Creation at the beginning, as far as this share is concerned, was no more than a kind of beginning for these created things, and potentialities for their completion — abilities to be completed, still waiting to be brought out; but their actual completion was handed over to man entirely.
Our Sages, of blessed memory, have already drawn our attention to the truth of this matter, for they said that everything that was created in the work of Creation needs perfecting: wheat needs grinding, lupines need sweetening — soaking out their bitterness — and so with all of them (Bereshit Rabbah 11:6). And we find further that Turnus Rufus — the Roman governor of Judea — asked Rabbi Akiva, Which works are finer, those of Heaven or those of flesh and blood? And he answered him, Those of flesh and blood are finer. And to prove his words he brought him ears of grain and fine loaves, and said to him, Which of these are finer? (Tanchuma, Tazria 5) — the grain as Hashem made it, or the bread that man made from it?
And indeed, our own eyes see that all natural things, when they are left to their nature without man's labor and craft, will indeed do some of what is in their natural law, but not completely; and when man works with them and helps their nature, and arranges what they bring forth in the proper order, they will clearly be seen to be more complete and finer; and this is obvious. For example, any tree, if it is left to its nature without cultivation, even if it gives of the kind of fruit that is its own, will not equal, neither in its taste nor in its beauty, what it would give if it were cultivated; and the soil itself, when it is not worked, not fertilized and not hoed, either does not give its produce at all, or gives it lean and lacking — except for a few places where the natural readiness of the soil is abundant to a great degree, so that they need no working; and this is not at all the usual case. The sum of the matter: the Creator, blessed be He, left room for mankind, in whatever their hand can reach, for them to distinguish themselves in it, by raising up through their toil what nature brings forth. Now, the same thing happens also to the mind of man himself: although understanding is implanted in it by its nature from the start, if it is not cultivated it will be like a tree that is not cultivated, and like soil that no one has taken care of; for even though it will not cease to understand many things, just as the tree does not cease to give of its own fruit, yet its understanding after it has been cultivated is not to be compared with its understanding without this, just as the fruit of the cultivated tree is not to be compared with its fruit without this.
And just as it needs study of the subjects of existence — the things that exist — that is, all the things the mind understands, which are its occupation, and without this its understanding would not go out from potential to actual — from an ability it has to knowledge it really holds — so it needs study of understanding itself, that is, of the right way to think, so that its understanding of the things it understands will be a complete and orderly understanding, and not lacking and confused. And indeed, for this purpose the wise men who came before us took pains to set out the orders of understanding and to explain its laws correctly, by looking at what happens to the mind in its acts of understanding — grasping and ignorance, a true conception and a false one, that is, a true or a false picture of a thing in the mind — in order to know what it must guard against in its reflection so as not to err, and by what it may be helped so as to grasp the truth. And the whole of this study is what is called the craft of logic.
And when I saw the great need that we truly have for this, for without it one cannot enter the inner chambers of the branches of wisdom and delight in their pleasures as is fitting, I chose to set out this study in brief, as much as I saw to be necessary for the subject to be complete. Most of it I translated from books that preceded me in other languages, and brought it into our language, to benefit the children of our people. And matters I added, removed and changed, compared with what I found before me, as seemed to me more fitting.
I beg you, pleasant reader, stand still and consider (Iyov 37:14); listen and increase learning (Mishlei 1:5), and knowledge will be pleasant to your soul (Mishlei 2:10).

The craft of logic in general: what it is, and the need for it. The division of existing things into the perceived by the senses and the intelligible; and of the intelligible into the abstracted and the imagined; and of the imagined into the apprehended and the fictitious.
(1) Now, all the labor of the mind and all its effort is to grasp things as they truly are. Yet there are times when it happens to err in them, and what it grasps of them is false; therefore it needs study, so as to know how to recognize the places of stumbling where it may stumble, and to know how to guard itself against them, until its grasping is true. And the whole of this study is what is called the craft of logic.

(2) The chief work of the mind, in its seeking the knowledge of things, is discernment: until it recognizes each and every thing by itself, discerned and set apart from everything else. But since, among all existing things, there are respects in which one resembles another, and there are respects in which one is set apart from another, therefore the mind will not reach the end of its work until it is perfected in the two activities, which are likening and distinguishing — seeing how things are alike, and seeing how they differ.

(3) In each one of the two activities error can occur: if it likens what is not alike, or sets apart what is not set apart. Therefore both of them need study and training and orderly rules, which will keep it on the straight path, and it will not stray from it, until it attains its purpose properly.

(4) All existing things divide into two parts. The first: the perceived by the senses, or the sensed; and the second: the intelligible — a thing grasped by the mind alone. The perceived by the senses is what is grasped by one of the senses; the intelligible is what the mind pictures in its imagination, but its existence is not so outside of it — outside the mind it does not stand by itself as the mind pictures it. And it too is divided into two: the one abstracted, and the other imagined.
Its explanation: the sensed is, for example, the stone and the tree, which one sees with the senses; and the intelligible — such as wisdom, memory, strength, which are things that one understands and conceives in the mind, but the senses do not see them.

(5) The abstracted is this: that what is not grasped by the senses except joined with something else, the mind separates it in its imagination and takes it by itself. The imagined is what is not grasped by the senses at all, neither by itself nor joined to something else, but it is the mind that pictures it; and it too divides into two: the first, apprehended, and the second, fictitious.
Its explanation: appearance — that is, whiteness and blackness and the other colors — the senses do not see them by themselves, but only as they are set in one of the bodies; yet the mind conceives whiteness as being one thing, added to the body that it is in; and this is called separating it in its imagination from the body in which it is set, and this is the abstracted. But the imagined is not so, and it will be explained in the section before us — the next paragraph.

(6) The apprehended is the thing that, although its existence is not present in what is sensed, is fit to exist according to the order of steps, by which the more general comes before the more particular, and the sensed follows from it in order; and the fictitious is what is neither present nor fit to be, nor does the sensed follow from it in order.
Its explanation: the apprehended is that from what we see with the senses we judge of an existence that we do not see. For example: we see that there are human beings, and they are living; beasts, and they too are living; birds, and they too are so; so we say that there is one kind of creature among the creatures, which is called the kind of living creatures; and this kind is not a thing actually present apart from these particulars of it that we mentioned — the individual men, beasts and birds — but the mind pictures it as though there were one general thing that divides into particular parts, because it belongs to the order of steps that there be the general and afterwards the particular, like the tree and its branches; and so it turns out that the sensed follows, step by step, from the imagined, as though that imagined thing were the root and the sensed things branches from it. That is not so with the fictitious, which is imagination alone, and there is nothing among the sensed things from which we may judge that that fictitious thing exists.

The substance and the accident, and its rules
(1) Up to here we have explained the matters of grasping and its divisions; now we shall explain the things grasped, by their divisions — what kinds of things there are for the mind to grasp.

(2) Everything grasped is either a substance or an accident. Its explanation: whether among the things grasped that are sensed or those that are intelligible, which were explained above — this division holds of both.

(3) A substance is the real thing whose standing is in itself and not in another — it exists on its own, not as something found in another thing — and in it stand the accidents that join it. Its explanation: for example, the substance of the stone, the tree, the living creature, and all existing things, spiritual and physical.

(4) An accident is a matter that is found in a substance and stands in it, and cannot stand without a substance. For example, appearance, which we mentioned above, beauty, wisdom, which are not found by themselves, but are set in one of the substances — a color is always the color of some thing, and wisdom is always the wisdom of someone. The rules of the accident:
1. The existence of an accident is its being joined to a substance. Its explanation: for the accident is nothing but a matter of being in a substance: one aspect, or many aspects, added to its being a substance. The being of that aspect, found in a substance — this is the accident that happened to the substance.
2. The accident depends on the substance both in coming to be and in existence — in its continuing to be. Its explanation: if there were no substance, there would be no aspect added to it, and it would turn out that there was no accident at all; therefore we say that the accident depends on the substance in coming to be. And likewise, if it — the substance — ceased to be, the accident would not be happening; therefore we say that the accident depends on the substance in existence.
3. An accident without a substance is impossible.
4. The accident does not pass from subject to subject — from one thing that bears it to another — or from substance to substance. Its explanation: for the substance bears many accidents, and may bear one accident at one time and afterwards bear another accident, and the substance that bore the one is the one that bears the second. But the accident that happens to a substance cannot go out of it and join another substance; rather, what happened to the one has already come to an end with its absence from it, and what happens to another substance is a new thing, and not the first.

Quantity, continuous and discrete. Quality and its four kinds. The acquired state and its three kinds. The theoretical and its three kinds. Nature, and what is beyond nature. The sciences of measure. Ethics, statecraft and livelihood. The free crafts and the crafts not free. Natural readiness. Primary and secondary makeup. Natural and crafted form. The rules of quality. Action and its rules. Being acted upon and its rules. Relation and its rules. Time, place, position and possession. Particulars and universals. Genus and species. Highest and intermediate genus, remote and near. The rules of the genus and the rules of the species. The distinguishing feature and its rules. The distinctive property and its rules, and the accident.
(1) We have already explained the accident in general; now we shall explain its parts.
(2) The parts of the accident are nine, and they are: quantity, quality, action, being acted upon, relation, time, position, possession, place (literally, "where").

(3) Quantity is an accident by which a thing is measured, and on its account one asks, "How much?" — in Hebrew kamah, from which quantity, kamut, takes its name. And it divides into two parts: the one, measure, which they — the logicians — called continuous quantity; and the second, number, which they called discrete quantity.
Its explanation: for the many parts and their cleaving to one another make a body with a size that can be measured; and this is what they meant in saying "continuous quantity" (literally, "cleaving quantity"). And their being many, separate from one another, gives rise to number, and this is what they meant in calling it "discrete quantity" (literally, "separate quantity").

(4) Quality is an accident by which one says of a thing "what" and "how" — what sort of thing it is and how it is; quality, eichut, takes its name from eich, "how." It divides into four kinds: the acquired state and natural readiness, makeup and form.

(5) The acquired state is a quality in a person through which he is fit for certain actions — a knowledge or skill that he has gained — and it divides into three kinds: theoretical, practical and technical.
(6) The theoretical is that whose matter is knowledge and grasping — knowing, for the sake of knowing — and its kinds are three: nature, what is beyond nature, and the sciences of measure.

(7) Nature is the knowledge of natural things considered as natural, and grasped by the senses — what is called natural science; what is beyond nature is the knowledge of the things that are above all the senses and are not grasped by them — what is called metaphysics. The sciences of measure: included in them are the wisdom of the spheres — the science of the heavenly bodies — arithmetic, geometry, optics — the science of sight — music, and the like.

(8) The practical is the knowledge of setting conduct right, and it divides into three kinds, and they are: ethics, statecraft, and livelihood — the right conduct of a person's own character, of a state, and of a household and its earnings.
(9) The technical is the knowledge of some craft, and it divides into two: free crafts — what are called the liberal arts — and the second, those not free.

(10) The free ones are those fitting for princes and nobles, and they are three: grammar, rhetoric — the art of persuasive speech — and logic. The ones not free are those not fitting for princes and nobles, such as sewing, building, weaving and the like.

(11) Natural readiness is that which is found in the subject — the one who has it — by reason of his nature, not acquired by him; such as sharpness of mind and of memory, strength of body and its health, quickness of movement.

(12) Makeup is what is in the inner content of a thing and its blend — the mixture of heat and cold, moisture and dryness, out of which bodies are made — and it divides into two: the one primary, and the second secondary.

(13) The primary divides into four, and they are: heat and cold, moisture and dryness; and the secondary — such as hardness and softness, lightness and heaviness, and the like — which come about from the mixture of the primary ones.
(14) Form is the form of the thing — its outward shape — by which it is seen and pictured in the mind; and it divides into two: the one natural, and the second crafted.

(15) The natural: the form of a man, the form of a horse, and so the other species; the crafted: the form of what is made by human hands.
The rules of quality: 1. In quality there can be less and more — one thing may be whiter or wiser than another. 2. Among the qualities there is contrariety — some of them are contraries, opposite ends of one range. For example: heat and cold. 3. By reason of quality, things are said to be alike and not alike — two things are called alike when they share a quality, as two white garments.

(16) Action is the stirring of the substance, or the revealing and going out of the active power that is in the substance. (Or say: the drawing forth of the effect from the acting cause, as we said above. For example: heating is the drawing forth of heat from the fire.)
The rules of action: 1. Everyone who acts by will acts for some purpose. 2. In actions there is less and more. 3. In action there can be contrariety. For example: warming, cooling.

(17) Being acted upon is the impression of the action — the mark the action leaves in the thing it acts on.
The rules of being acted upon: 1. In being acted upon there is less and more. 2. In being acted upon there can be contrariety — being warmed and being cooled.

(18) Relation is a kind of connection between two things, on account of which it is said of one of them that it belongs to the other. Its explanation: for example, a father, which is a thing related to a son; and a son is a thing related to a father. For there is no father unless he has a son, and there is no son unless he has a father.
The rules of relation: 1. The accident of relation exceeds all the accidents in its abundance — every thing stands in many relations to other things: greater and smaller, earlier and later, near and far. 2. The two related things are necessarily equal in absence and in existence. Its explanation: when the one is found to exist, the second is necessary; and likewise, when the one is absent, the ceasing of the second is necessary. For there is no father unless he has a son; and if there is a father, there is certainly a son; and if there is no father, there is no son.
(19) Time is an accident of time in the substance, that is: the measure of its distance from the beginning or the end — how long since it began, or how long until it ends.
(20) Place (literally, "where") is an accident of place in the substance, that is: the part of the world that is filled by it.

(21) Position is an accident of position in the substance. Its explanation: the manner in which the parts of the substance are found in a place — this is what is called position; such as standing, sitting, reclining, and the like.

(22) Possession is an accident that indicates a kind of acquisition acquired by the substance, or a clothing upon it. (The Hebrew uses the same word, kinyan, for this and for the acquired state among the qualities.) For example: the garments that are on a person, or the traits acquired in his soul — humility, generosity, and the like.

(23) These ten general classes of things that we have mentioned — one substance and nine accidents — under them are included all the things of existence, according to their levels. These ten are what are called the categories.
(24) And the things examined in the ten classes that we mentioned are two, and they are: the particulars and the universals — each single thing, and the general classes that take in many things.
(25) The particulars are the things that exist, each one by itself, such as a man among the men, a bird among the birds, a tree among the trees, and the like; and they are called individuals.
(26) The universals are two: first, the universals of existence; and the second, their attendants — things that come along with them.
(27) The universals of existence are also two: the first, genus, and the second, species — a wider class, and a narrower class within it.

(28) Genus and species are one in their nature: it is a general class that takes in particulars by reason of a sharing, in that they share in one thing. And the difference between the genus and the species is that what includes more is called a genus, and what includes only some of what is included in the genus is called a species.
For example: living creatures is a genus, for included in it are the animals and the birds, the fish and human beings, by reason of what they share in the matter of life: they are all living. But the class of human beings is called a species, for it too includes all the individual human beings, that is, Reuven, Shimon and so on, but it does not include the animals and the birds and the fish, which were included in the name "living creatures."
(29) The genus divides into highest or intermediate, remote and near.

(30) The highest genus is one that has no other genus above it; its explanation: none that includes more than it — such as the ten categories. The intermediate is one that has a genus more inclusive than it, so that in relation to that one the intermediate genus is called a species, and in relation to the species beneath it, it is called a genus.

(31) A remote genus is one that is far from the species, and a near one, one that is near to it. Its explanation: the genus of the genus is remote from the species, for there is another level between it and the species. For example: the rooster is a species among the species of birds; bird is a genus to the species of birds; living creatures is the genus of the genus to the rooster, and is called a remote genus; and bird is called a near genus. The rules of the genus: 1. The genus is greater than each and every species beneath it. Its explanation: for the genus is what includes many species. 2. The genus is not separated from its species. Its explanation: for the genus is nothing but the general law common to its species — the description that fits them all — and so it turns out that no species can be without this law. 3. What happens to the genus happens to every species — whatever is true of all living creatures is true of the birds as well. 4. When a genus is posited — set down as existing — species are necessarily posited; and when the genus is absent, they are all absent.
The rules of the species: 1. The species is born from the genus's being limited by certain distinguishing features, by which one species is told apart from another species. For example: from the genus of living creatures the species of man is born when the distinguishing feature of speech is joined to it, and we say: a speaking living creature. 2. The species is later by nature than its genus — not later in time, but in that it depends on the genus, and the genus does not depend on it. 3. When a species is posited, the genus is necessarily posited; but when one species is absent, the absence of the genus is not necessary — were there no birds, there would still be living creatures.
(32) The attendants of the universals are three: distinguishing feature, distinctive property and accident.

(33) A distinguishing feature is an essential matter — a part of what the thing is — by which two things that share in a genus or in a species are told apart from each other. It turns out that the genus and the species make known, of the essence of the existing thing, what it shares with others, and the distinguishing feature makes known of it what sets it apart from others.
For example: man and beast share in life, and the distinguishing feature of man from the beast is speech. And man is called a speaking living creature, and the beast, a living creature that does not speak.
The rules of the distinguishing feature: The distinguishing feature is an essential matter belonging only to the genus or to its species, and it is found in it, in most of it, and at all times. For example: speech is essential to the species of man, for without it he would not be a man; and it is found in most of the species and at all times.

(34) A distinctive property is a distinguishing feature that is not essential, that is, it makes known of the existing thing that by which it is told apart from others, but it is not of its essence. For example: laughter, for the species of man; for it is found only in him, yet it is not of his essence, for his being a man does not depend on it, since without this he would be a man.
The rules of the distinctive property: The distinctive property belongs only to the species or to the genus, and it is found in most of it and at all times, and it is not essential to it.

(35) The accident — here, as one of the three attendants — is a matter in an existing thing that neither belongs to it alone nor is essential to it — such as whiteness in a man.
The rules of the accident: The accident is found in a minority of the genus or species, and not at all times, and it is not essential to it. The other matters of the accident were explained above — in the second chapter.

The three acts of the mind. The name of one meaning, and the synonymous. The absolutely shared. The shared with a relation: general, borrowed, transferred, known. Names that serve logic. The cause and its rules. The maker and the purpose: the maker in itself and the maker by accident; the maker alone and in partnership. Makers of equal weight and not of equal weight; the necessary partnership and the one not necessary. The rousing cause and the instrumental; the generating, the sustaining and the destroying. Natural and voluntary action. The remote cause and the proximate.
(1) Until now we have explained the occupation of logic — what it deals with; now we shall explain its division into its sections, and they are three: the first, the explanation of names; the second, the explanation of statements — sentences that say something about something; the third, syllogisms — reasonings that draw a conclusion from two statements.
Its explanation: the acts of the mind are three. The first is grasping the subjects that come before it, just as they come — taking in each thing simply, before saying anything about it. For example: the stone, the tree, the iron, and the like. The second is joining to a subject — the thing spoken about — what is affirmed of it or denied of it, so that out of this the statement is built. For example: "The tree is large" — he has affirmed largeness of the tree; "This paper is not white" — he has denied whiteness of the paper. The third is joining statement to statement, and bringing forth from them another, so that there are three. For example: "Man is a living creature; Reuven is a man; if so, he is a living creature." For the first act the mind makes use of names; for the second, of statements; for the third, of syllogisms. Its explanation: a syllogism is the joining of statements and the bringing forth of their conclusion.

(2) A name signifies one of the substances or one of the accidents — a thing that stands by itself, or a quality found in a thing — and it is divided according to its signification — the way it points to what it means — and according to its content. According to its signification its divisions are three: of one meaning, synonymous, shared.
Its explanation: there are names that signify a matter in a simple way, and some that signify by way of likeness, and some that signify by way of agreement — because people have agreed to use them so — as I shall write further on. And in this respect the names are examined according to their signification. But the names are examined further with respect to the matters hinted at in them, as we shall write further on. Now, with respect to signification, the name is divided into these three: of one meaning, and so on.

(3) The name of one meaning is one that alone signifies one matter only; the synonymous is when there are many names signifying one matter: each one of them is called synonymous. An example of the name of one meaning: the name of a substance, such as Avraham, Moshe, Yerushalayim; a name of relation — naming a man by the people he belongs to — such as "Hebrew," "Egyptian," and the like; a name of number: one, two. An example of the synonymous: lechem and pat, both words for bread.
(4) The shared name is one name that signifies many matters, and it is divided into two: the absolutely shared and the shared with a relation.

(5) The absolutely shared is one that signifies two matters between which there is no relation or likeness at all. For example: saf, which means a vessel — a basin — and means a doorpost.
The shared with a relation is one that signifies two matters between which there is some relation and likeness; and it is divided into four: general, borrowed, transferred, known.

(6) The general name is a name that signifies many matters, each one of them fit for this name just as it fits its fellow, equally, because they are all branches from one root; that is, the species under the genus, and the individuals under the species — the genus being a wide class, such as "living creature," and the species a kind within it, such as "man." For example: Reuven, Shimon, Levi — each one of them is called "man," because they are individuals of the species man; and the name "man" is called a general name.

(7) The borrowed name is a name that signifies one matter in a first signification, and another matter in a second signification, because it has some likeness to the first matter. Its explanation: "first signification" is the name for how the word is used in the language most of the time, and "second signification," how it is used at times. For example: "fire." Its first signification is the burning substance that we know; and in a second signification it signifies one who is very quick in his movement and is never still: we call him "fire" for the likeness he has to real fire, which moves quickly and is never still.

(8) The transferred name is a name that signifies two matters equally, because of a likeness between them, so that we cannot say of either one of them that it is a second signification. Its explanation: it has long been the custom in the language to use it so, that it signifies the two matters equally. For example: gader, "fence." It is understood of the built fence that is made around the fields, just as it is understood, among the logicians, of the complete explanation and true conception of a thing — its definition, which fences the thing in.
And so are all the names of grammar and logic and the other branches of wisdom, which took names to explain their laws because of the likeness they have to what the words signify in their first signification.

(9) The known name is a name that is said of many equally, and particularly of one, because that quality is stronger in him than in the others. And the thing is known to all, that what is meant by that name is that particular one. For example: "the mighty man," said without more, is said of Shimshon, even though this name belongs to every mighty man, because he excelled in might; "the singer" is said of David, even though there are many singers, because he excelled in song.

(10) Names, according to the matters hinted at in them, are divided into two: those of speech and those of study. Those of speech are the ones that serve for speaking, so that the speaker may mention by them what is in his thought of the things that exist; those of study are the ones particular to the branches of wisdom or to the crafts, through which one reaches the purpose intended in those branches of wisdom or crafts; and they are of twenty-two kinds, according to the kinds of the branches of wisdom and the crafts.

(11) The names that serve logic are twenty-one, and these are they: cause and effect; subject and the attached — what is joined to the subject; whole and part; derivation and derived; definition and defined; formation and formed; division and divided; things compared; things unlike; contraries; testimony and attested; genus and species.
Its explanation: these are the names by which we shall reach the purpose intended in logic, which is to know things as they truly are, in all the distinctions there are to be drawn in them.

(12) The cause is the thing by whose power the effect exists.
The rules of the cause: 1. The cause always precedes its effect, at least with a natural precedence. Its explanation: precedences are two, precedence of time and natural precedence. That of time is precedence in time; and the natural is when, even though what naturally precedes is together in time with what comes after it, still a precedence is understood for it in the mind, for if it did not exist, what comes after it would have no existence; and this is the precedence that is always found in a cause with respect to its effect; but in most things the cause precedes its effect in time as well. For example: the rising of the sun and the light of day come to be at one time. But since the existence of the light of day depends on the existence of the sun's rising, we call it preceding, and the light of day later by nature.
2. Nothing exists without a cause that brings it into existence. 3. In the causes there is no going on without end — one cause behind another forever. Its explanation: the highest cause is the Creator, blessed be His Name, above whom there is no cause.
4. If a cause is posited in actuality, the effect is posited as well; but when it is removed, only the effect is removed — the future effect, still to come, not the past. Its explanation: for example, a fire that heated iron: even if the fire goes out, the heat will not leave the iron, but no further heating will come from it. And further on we shall explain that this holds only for the proximate cause — the cause right next to its effect.

(13) The cause is divided into external and internal. The external is that which is outside the substance of the effect — not part of the thing itself. And it too is divided into two: the maker and the purpose — what brings the thing about, and what it is for.

(14) The maker is that through which the existing thing comes to be; and its kinds are two: a maker in itself, and a maker by accident — one that brings about its effect by chance, not by its own working.
(15) The maker in itself is one that acts by its nature or by its will; and it is divided into principal and secondary.

(16) The principal is the one on which the effect chiefly depends; and it is divided into a maker alone and a maker in company or in partnership. For example: the principal in the governing of the people — the king — while the ministers and officers rule under him.

(17) The maker alone is one that brings the effect into being by itself, without there being another equal to it in this bringing into being. Its explanation: "the maker alone" does not exclude the instrumental cause — the tool it works with — which we shall explain below, with the help of Heaven, for it is not equal to it in bringing the effect into being, but is beneath it in rank; but it excludes there being another equal to it in bringing the effect into being, at one rank with it.
(18) The maker in company is one that helps another in bringing the effect into being, on an equal footing with it. And the partners can be of equal weight or not of equal weight.

(19) Those of equal weight are those in which the share of each one of them is equal in bringing the effect into being; and those not of equal weight, those in which each one of them is not equal. And in either case, their partnership can be necessary or not necessary.
(20) A necessary partnership is when no one of them alone can bring its effect into being; and one not necessary, when one of them has the power to bring its effect into being by itself.
(21) The secondary cause is one whose power in bringing the effect into being is not the principal one; and it is divided into the rousing and the instrumental.

(22) The rousing cause is one that rouses the principal to act. For example: the desire for profit is what rouses the merchant to toil at his trade. The instrumental is one that serves the making cause to bring its effect into being. For example: the axe to the hewer.
(23) Further, the making cause is divided into three kinds: generating, sustaining and destroying.
(24) The generating cause is one that makes the effect new and brings it into being; the sustaining, one that makes it endure; and the destroying, one that brings it to nothing.

(25) Further, the making cause is divided into natural, and voluntary or by choice. The natural is one that acts because of its nature, by necessity; the voluntary, one that acts because of deliberation and choice, in that it is under no compulsion. For example: the burning of fire is a natural action, and it cannot do otherwise; a man's writing is voluntary.

(26) Further, it is divided — and so too all the other causes, which we shall explain with the help of Heaven — into remote, near and proximate. Between the remote and the effect there are many intermediaries; between the near and the effect, one; between the proximate and the effect, nothing at all. For example: Avraham is a remote cause of Reuven; Yitzchak, a near cause; Yaakov, a proximate cause.
The rules of the proximate cause: When the proximate cause is posited in actuality, the effect must exist in actuality; which is not so with the remote, nor with the near.
(27) The cause that makes by accident is one from which the effect is born neither from nature nor from will; and it is found both among the natural causes and among those of choice.

(28) A cause making by accident in natural things is one that acts not on account of its nature, but on account of an accident that befell it — a quality it happens to have. An example of the accidental in natural things: white paper tires the eyes on account of the accident of whiteness in it — not because it is paper.
(29) The accidental among things of choice is one that acts without intention, or in error.

The principal and the secondary purpose. Last and intermediate. The rules of the purpose.
(1) Until now we have explained the making cause; now we shall explain the purposive cause, and it is that for whose sake the effect comes about, or the thing is done; and it is divided into principal and secondary. The principal is the first intention of the maker; the secondary is the intention he has besides the first, at a rank second to it.

(2) Further, it is divided into last and intermediate. The last is as its name implies: the one with which the maker is satisfied, seeking nothing beyond it; the intermediate is one that is a purpose for one thing, but is a means to reach a further purpose that the maker had in mind. For example: the purpose of the wisdom of medicine is to know the diseases in their kinds, with their causes; but the last purpose is to heal the sick. The rules of the purposive cause: 1. The purpose moves the maker to act. 2. In one thing many purposes can be found.
3. The purposes make the actions different. Its explanation: one action, done by one maker for one purpose and by another maker for another purpose, is reckoned as different actions; and indeed one of them may be good and the other bad, even though the two of them are one, because their purposes are two. For example: two men lengthen their prayer, one for the sake of Heaven, and one to deceive people so that they will trust him; this one performs a great mitzvah, and that one incurs great guilt.
4. The purpose precedes its means in thought, which is not so in deed. Its explanation: no man thinks about the means unless he has thought at the start about the purpose, for whose sake those means are needed; but in deed it is impossible to reach the purpose except after all the means.
5. Once the purpose has come to be, the action that is done to reach it is at an end. Whoever truly wants the purpose must want the means. Its explanation: attaining the purpose without means is impossible.

Remote and near matter. The rules of matter. Essential and accidental form. The rules of form.
(1) Until now the external cause has been explained; now we shall explain the internal, which enters into the existence of the effect itself; and it is divided into two: matter and form — what a thing is made of, and what makes it the thing it is.

(2) Matter is that from which the effect is made; and it is divided into remote and near. The remote is that from which the effect is made together with another matter nearer than it; the near, that from which the effect is made with no matter in between. An example: the remote matter in man is the dust, for the child is not formed from dust directly; rather, the beginning of his being is dust; but the near matter is flesh and blood and the rest of what he is composed of.
The rules of matter: Matter precedes form by nature — not necessarily in time, but in the order of what depends on what. Its explanation: it is impossible for a form to exist except in matter.

(3) Form is that by which the effect is what it is; and it is divided into the essential and exact, and the accidental or inexact. The essential is that which makes the effect what it is in the truth of its being, and sets it apart from all other existing things. For example: the form of man is the speaking power, which includes the intellect and the will; for by this he is set apart in his essence.

(4) The inexact is a group of some accidents particular to some existing thing, by which we conceive it, when its essential form is not known. For example, that we say: "The dog is that which has the power of barking"; and this is not the root of what the dog is. The rules of form: 1. Form is always more honorable than matter. Its explanation: on it depends the whole truth of the existing thing's being, which is not so with matter. 2. The essential form is not grasped by the senses — only by the mind. 3. The actions of an existing thing depend on its form.

The effects of the four causes. The rules of the effect.
(1) Until now we have explained the cause; now we shall explain the effect, and it is what is born of the power of the cause.

(2) Each of the four causes has an effect — the maker, the purpose, the form and the matter. The effect of the making cause is the thing made; the effect of the purposive cause is the thing decreed — what was resolved upon for that purpose; the effect of the formal cause is the thing formed; the effect of the material cause is the matter — the thing as it is made of its matter. The rules of the effect: 1. The effect will not have more power than its cause. Its explanation: the effect is nothing but what is born of the cause, and the cause cannot bring forth what is not in it; if so, it is impossible for there to be in the effect what is not found in its cause.
2. As the essence of the cause, so is the essence of the effect. Its explanation: this is to be understood only of natural causes that are principal and specific, and of an effect that is able to receive the essence of its cause — as fire kindles fire.
3. The thing on whose account another is what it is — all the more so is it itself such. For example: if books are precious on account of the wisdom engraved in them, all the more so is the wisdom itself precious.

The subject and the object. The subject absolute and limited. Exclusive and not exclusive.
(1) The subject — literally "that which bears" — is the thing to which something is joined, that is, the thing that carries some quality or some act, and it is divided into subject and object. The subject in this narrower sense is that which receives something in it, or upon it. For example: fire is a subject to heat, for the heat is received in the fire. An object — that with which one who is occupied is occupied; that is, the thing toward which an act is directed, without the act being received in it. For example: what is seen — the object of seeing. The thing seen bears the act of seeing in the sense that the seeing is about it, but the seeing is not lodged in it as heat is lodged in the fire.

(2) The subject is divided into absolute and limited. The absolute is one to which the attached thing — the quality that joins it — is joined without any limit or condition. For example: fire, to which heat is joined absolutely, in all of it and in every respect. The limited — one to which the attached thing is joined only according to one matter or one respect. For example: the Kushite, the dark-skinned man, is a subject to whiteness not with respect to the whole of him, but with respect to one of his parts, namely the teeth. One may say truly that he is white, but only in this limited sense.

(3) Further, the subject is divided into exclusive or not exclusive. The exclusive is one that is bound to its accident alone, that is, to the quality that it bears, so that this one is not found without that one. For example: heat and fire are not found one without the other. The one that is not exclusive is one that is not bound alone with its accident, but that accident is found also in something other than it. For example: the living creature and being visible; for every living creature is visible, but there is a visible thing that is not a living creature, such as a stone. Here the living creature is a subject of being visible, yet it does not hold that quality alone.

The attached: inherent and adjacent. The stationary and the moving. The preceding and the following. The predicate, essential and accidental; in potential and in actuality. The rules of the attached.
(1) The attached is that which is joined to a subject — the quality or thing that the subject bears, as explained in the previous chapter — and it is divided into inherent and adjacent: what is joined within the subject, and what only stands beside it.

(2) The inherent is that which is joined within a subject and cannot exist without it, and it is divided into exclusive and not exclusive. The exclusive is that which is found only in subjects of one species, and it is divided into complete and incomplete.

(3) The complete exclusive is that which is found in the whole of its subject and at all times, and not in anything other than it. For example: sensation to a living creature; every living creature senses, always, and nothing but a living creature senses.

(4) The incomplete is that which is found in one subject exclusively, but with something missing. Its meaning: not in anything other than it, but not in the whole of it, or not at every time. For example: laughter is exclusive to man, for it is not found in anything other than him, but it is not in man at every time.

(5) The one that is not exclusive is that which is found in subjects of different species. For example: moving from place to place, which is found in man, and is found as well in animals, and also in inanimate things, as a stone that falls.

(6) The adjacent — what is joined to the subject from outside it — is divided into stationary and moving. The stationary — either it rests upon the subject itself, or it is found together with it, or it surrounds and bounds it. For example: the garment rests upon the body; with the birth of Moshe there was found together with it the filling of the house with light (Sotah 12a); time bounds the action that is done on such-and-such a day, at such-and-such an hour. The moving goes before the subject, or comes after it; therefore it is divided into preceding and following. For example: the spring precedes the summer, and the season of ingathering comes after it.
(7) Further, the attached, or the predicate — what is said of the subject — is divided into essential and accidental.

(8) The essential is exclusive to the subject according to its essential form, that is, it follows from what the subject is, and it is found in it for the most part; the accidental is that which is not exclusive to it, and is found in it only in its minority — in only a few of the subject's instances. An example of the essential: heat to fire. An example of the accidental: whiteness to the garment, for a garment is a garment whatever its color.
(9) Further, the existence of the predicate in the subject is divided into two: the one in potential and the second in actuality.

(10) Existence in potential is for as long as the predicate is in the subject in readiness alone, and is not in deed; in actuality — when it has come to deed. An example of potential: a man has it in his power to be a writer even at a time when he is not writing; and at the time that he is writing he is called: a writer in actuality.

(11) Potential is divided into remote and near. The remote is that which lacks many stages before it can exist in actuality, as a young child who has not yet learned his letters is a writer in remote potential; the near is that which lacks nothing but the stage of its going out into actuality, as a scribe who has learned his craft and needs only to take up the pen. The rules of the attached:
1. The accident that is exclusive to one species cannot be ascribed to another species that is not like it. For example: knowledge is exclusive to the species of man; it will not be ascribed to stones.
2. The complete exclusive accident does not part from its subject even for one moment.
3. It is impossible to conceive a subject while denying its complete exclusive accident; one cannot picture a living creature that does not sense.
4. The attached is said of the subject in conjunction, not absolutely. Its meaning is that when the attached is said to be a predicate in its subject, it is understood by this that it is one of the accidents, cleaving to the subject, so that its subject is described by it; and this is what is called by the grammarians an adjective, such as wise, mighty. We say "Reuven is wise," and not "Reuven is wisdom." But the accident taken absolutely is what the grammarians have called a noun, in which the subject is not described by the accident, such as wisdom, might; these name the quality itself, apart from any one who bears it.

The essential whole and the accidental; composite and built. The uniform and the not uniform. The rules of the whole. The part and its rules.
(1) A whole is that which is joined together from parts out of which it is built, and it is divided into a whole in its own right and an accidental whole.
(2) A whole in its own right is that which has in it real parts that build it, and it is divided into composite, or essential, and built.

(3) The composite, or essential, is that whose parts are essential to it, namely matter and form: the stuff a thing is made of, and the form that makes that stuff into this particular thing. Its meaning: every existing thing that is composed of matter and form, with respect to its being a compound of these two, is called an essential whole. These parts cannot be set side by side or taken apart by hand; they are distinguished only by the mind.
(4) The built is that which has building parts from whose joining together it is built, parts that can be found and pointed to, and it is divided into uniform and not uniform.

(5) The uniform is one in which every part of it is like the whole in name and in nature. For example: fire; every part of a fire is also called fire, and has the nature of fire. The not uniform is one in which not every part of it is like the whole in name and in nature. For example: a man or a house, of which not every part is called a man or a house; a hand is not a man, nor is a wall a house.

(6) The accidental whole is one that is not an essential whole, but only by way of accident. For example: the subject that is divided by its predicates; when we consider a man as made up of his qualities — tall, wise, white — he is a kind of whole and they are its parts, but they are not what he is in himself. The rules of the whole:
1. There is a difference between the whole and its parts, and even between the whole and all of them together, while they are still only parts. Its meaning is that when the parts are joined together and make one whole joined from all of them, there comes into being from this an existence that is not found at all even when they were all together but not joined. For example: if you arrange all the limbs of the animal one beside the other, they will not be called an animal, but the parts of an animal.
2. The whole, compared with its parts, is more complete, and the parts, compared with the whole, are more lacking.
3. When the whole is posited, that is, when we affirm that it is there, the parts are posited of necessity; but when the whole is denied, the denial of the parts is not made necessary. Where there is a house, there are walls; but where there is no house, there may still be walls standing on their own.

(7) The part is that from which the whole is built, in the company of two or more parts together, and its divisions are like the divisions of the whole. The rules of the part:
1. Every part, compared with the whole, is lacking.
2. Not all that the whole has does every part have; a man can see, but his hand cannot.
3. What the part has in its own right the whole has by virtue of that part which is in it; because the eye sees, the man is said to see.

Derivation and the derived, and their rules. Formation and its rules.
(1) Derivation is the explanation of a word and its source — from what the word was taken, and so why the thing bears that name.

(2) The derivations of words are taken from causes, from effects, from subjects, and from attached things, and from contraries: a thing may be named after what brought it about, after what it brings about, after what it rests in, after what is joined to it, or even after its opposite. For example: adam, man, from adamah, the earth, from which he was formed; Noach from menuchah, rest.

(3) A derived word is one that is built according to the derivation. The rules of derivation:
Not for all words is a derivation to be sought. Its meaning is that there are primary words, and they are those that are not derived from another word. For example: fire, water, bread.

(4) Formation is the way in which a word is built upon the foundation of its first meaning, the root from which its forms grow. For example: a noun, an adjective and an infinitive — all of them are built upon the foundation of the verb; namely zikkaron, remembrance, zachran, one who remembers well, zachor, to remember — all of them are kinds of formation upon the foundation zachor.
(5) The formed words are divided into adherent and absolute.

(6) The adherent are those that indicate one form in the subject, a quality that the subject bears, and that is the adjective. For example: wise, discerning, and the like. And the absolute — those that indicate one matter alone, without its subject being mentioned with it. For example: wisdom, discernment. The rules of formation:
1. When one of the ways of formation is posited, the others are posited; if there is wisdom, there is one who is wise.
2. What belongs to one of the ways of formation belongs to all of them. For example: if kindness is lovely, the kind man will be lovely.

The definition, the genus and the distinguishing feature. The requirements of the definition. The rules of the definition. Division, the divided, and their rules.
(1) A definition is a complete explanation of the thing defined, one that tells exactly what the thing is.
(2) In the definition one must consider the parts, the requirement, and the kind, each of which is now explained in turn.

(3) The parts of the definition are two: genus and distinguishing feature. The genus is the wider class to which the thing belongs together with others; the distinguishing feature is what sets it apart within that class. In the genus the thing defined is equal to others, and in the distinguishing feature it is set apart from all others. For example: the definition of man — a speaking living creature, that is, a living creature endowed with speech and reason; "living creature" — the genus in which he is equal with those that do not speak; "speaking" — this is the distinguishing feature by which he is set apart from them.

(4) The requirements of the definition are two. The one, that its words be fitting and clear; the second, that the definition be of the measure of the thing defined, so that it says neither less than what it is nor more than what it is. Its meaning: that nothing other than it should enter into it, and nothing of it should be missing from it. For example: if we define man as a living creature that walks on its two legs, behold, the birds enter into this, and the definition is too wide; or if we define the soul as the thing that wills and understands, behold, one part of the soul remains that is not mentioned in this, which is memory; and the definition is too narrow.

(5) The kinds of definition are two, complete and incomplete. The complete is that which is built of genus and distinguishing feature. The incomplete is one that explains the thing defined by way of what is not principal in it, not by what it is in itself, such as: the effect, the parts, the accompaniment, and the like. For example: if we define wine as the drink that intoxicates — by its effect; or if we define the date palm as the tree on which there are young shoots, fronds and dates — by its parts; or if we define the flame as the thing that smoke goes before — by what accompanies it. The rules of the definition:
1. Of whatever the definition is affirmed or denied, the thing defined is affirmed or denied; and so too the reverse. For example: of one of whom it is said that he is a speaking living creature, it is said that he is a man.
2. What belongs or does not belong to the definition belongs or does not belong to the thing defined. For example: what is said of a speaking living creature is said of man.
(6) Division is explaining the whole and distinguishing it into its parts, and it is divided into principal and not principal.

(7) The principal is the dividing of the whole into principal parts, and the not principal — into parts that are not principal; and these are the whole in its own right and the whole by accident mentioned above (chapter 10): a whole in its own right is divided into principal parts, an accidental whole into parts that are not principal.

(8) The requirements of principal division are two: first, that the parts be neither fewer nor more than the thing divided, but together exactly cover it; second, that the parts be alike with the whole and not alike among themselves: each part is a kind of the whole, and no part is contained in another. Its meaning: man and beast are parts of the sentient — the class of all that has sensation — that are not alike, but man and living creature are not unalike, for man is a living creature as well; so they may not be listed as two parts of one division. The rules of division:
1. Division must be into near parts. Its meaning: that you should not divide the genus into individuals when there are several species between the genus and them, but into the species that come immediately after it in the order of steps. One should not divide "living creature" straight into Reuven, Shimon and this horse, but first into man and beast.
2. Division must make the parts as few as possible.

(9) The divided — its aspects are like the aspects of division. The rules of the divided:
1. Whatever we wish to divide must first have removed from it all doubts and shared uses of language, that is, words with more than one meaning, lest we divide two different things as if they were one.
2. What is divided properly must of necessity have parts.

Things compared. The equal and their rules. The similar and their rules.
(1) Things compared, that is, things set side by side and measured one against the other, are alike either in genus, or in species, or in accidents. In genus the species are alike, as man and horse are both living creatures; in species — the individuals, as Reuven and Shimon are both men; in accidents — those that have one nature or one quantity, that is, the same kind of quality, or the same amount; and these are divided into the equal and the similar.

(2) The equal are those that are equal in the quantity of their quality, that is, they have the same quality in the same measure. For example, if we say, "Kindness is as much beloved as justice," the meaning in this is that there is as much reason in kindness for it to be beloved as there is in justice; and so kindness and justice are found to be equal in the quantity of this quality that is in them, namely, being beloved. The rules of the equal:
1. What applies to one of the equal applies to its fellow. Its meaning: this must be understood of what applies to one of them by virtue of the aspect that it has in which it is equal to its fellow. For example, justice: like kindness, because it is beloved, the perfect men command it, and this is because the perfect men's commanding it depends on its being beloved, which is the very thing in which the two are equal. However, if you say, "Kindness requires softness of heart," you will not infer on account of this that justice requires it; for this does not depend on that in which they are equal, which is being beloved, but on what kindness has in particular, according to its own nature.
2. Where one of the equal belongs, its fellow too will belong; whatever has room for the one has room for the other. For example: in the heart of one who seeks the good, kindness rests; if so, justice also.
3. Two that are equal to a third are equal to each other.
(3) The similar are similar either in quality, or in action and being acted upon.

(4) Likeness is simple or compound; the simple — between two; the compound — between four. For example: the simple — man and grass are alike in frailty, and there are here only two subjects; the compound — the ruler with his people is like the pilot with his ship, namely, in the matter of watching over and guiding; and the likeness is not completed except with four subjects: ruler and pilot, people and ship. The ruler is not like the pilot in himself, but as the ruler stands to his people, so the pilot stands to his ship. The rules of the similar:
1. Any two similar things must also be dissimilar. Its meaning is that likeness is not their being one, but their being two, with a likeness between them. If so, it is necessary that they be set apart by some difference, and then be alike in some likeness. For example, if you say, "Man is like the grass of the field," you will not on account of this infer that, if so, he grows from the soil, for he is only like grass in certain matters, but not in all.
2. What applies to one of the similar with respect to that in which it is alike applies also to its fellow. For example: narrow pipes and the entrances of understanding in children are equal, that is, alike in their narrowness; just as into the one, much water cannot enter at one time, so into the other, many things the mind understands cannot enter at one time; and so a child must be taught a little at a time.

The unlike, the different, the compared, the greater and the lesser. Their rules. The dissimilar and their rules. The absolute.
(1) The unlike are those in which what is in one is not in its fellow; and they are divided into the different and the contraries — the contraries, things so opposed that they cannot be found together, are the subject of the next chapter.

(2) The different are those that are set apart one from the other without a strong opposition, that is, they differ, yet nothing prevents them from being together; and they are divided into the compared and the absolute.

(3) The compared are those in which there is a difference in their measure, one against the other, when they are set side by side and weighed against each other; and they are divided into the differing and the dissimilar.

(4) The differing are those that differ in the quantity of their quality — they share one quality, but one has more of it and the other less — and they are the greater or the lesser.
The rules of the greater: 1. Whatever the greater applies to, the lesser applies to. For example: if the Master, blessed be He, creates something from nothing, which is the greater deed, all the more so that He is able to sustain what exists, which is the lesser. 2. What does not apply to the greater does not apply to the lesser, provided the relation is kept — that is, the same thing is said of both, in the same respect. Its explanation: let us say, for example, In His holy ones He does not trust (Iyov 15:15) — Hashem does not rely on the angels, who are greater than man; it is derived from this: all the more so does He not trust in human beings. And here the relation is kept, as regards both human beings and the holy ones: what we affirm of each will be the lack of His trust, blessed be He, in them.
The rules of the lesser: 1. Whatever the lesser does not apply to, the greater does not apply to. 2. What is required in the lesser, all the more so is it required in the greater.

(5) Further, one must distinguish between a thing's being lesser or greater and its being more possible, or not so possible — that is, more or less easily done.
Its explanation: if we say, It is greater to discover a new thing that the earlier ones did not know than to explain well what the earlier ones knew, it follows that the new discovery is the greater and the explanation the lesser. But you should not derive from this that the new discovery is more possible because it is greater, and the explanation not so possible; for every lesser thing, in itself, is more possible, and the new discovery, which is the greater, is in itself not so possible. The greater a deed, the harder it is to do.

(6) The dissimilar are the compared things that are set apart one from the other in their quality, and in action and being acted upon — not in having more or less of one thing, but in being of another sort. For example, if we say, Egypt is not like Shechem; a man is not like a wall.
The rules of the dissimilar: What applies to one of them does not apply to its fellow, in the respect in which it is dissimilar from it.
(7) The absolute are what is denied of some particular subject without comparison — the thing is simply said not to be so, without weighing it against another. For example: Some man is not white.

The contraries. Their rules. The opposites and their rules. The privatives and their rules. The distinguished. The conflicting and their rules. The correlatives and their rules.
(1) The contraries are those that are set apart one from the other by a strong opposition, so that it is impossible to unite them in one thing. For example: blackness and whiteness.
(2) What one must consider in the contraries is the distinctive property — what belongs to all contraries alone — and the species, that is, their kinds.

(3) The distinctive property of the contraries is that they will not be found in one subject, in one respect, in one part, at one time.
Its explanation: when one of these conditions is lacking, they can be found together. For example: a man can be white compared with one who is blacker than he, and be black compared with one who is whiter than he; and this is in different respects. Further, a man can be black, for example, in his skin and white in his teeth; and this is in different parts. Further, he can be black at one time and white at another time; and this is at different times.
The rules of the contraries: 1. Of whatever one of the contraries is affirmed, its fellow is denied. 2. Of whatever one of the contraries is denied, it is not necessary that its fellow be affirmed, unless they are contraries without a middle — with nothing that can stand between them. For example, if we say, This page is not white, it does not follow that it is black, for it can be green. But if you say, It is not day now, it must be night, for there is no middle between them. 3. Contrariety must be judged by the distinguishing feature, not by what is shared — two things are contraries only in what sets one apart from the other, not in what they have in common. For example, if we say, Man has sensation, it is not derived from it, then, that the living creature has no sensation, for sensation is shared by this one and that one. But if we say, Man invents crafts, we can derive from this, then, that the living creature does not invent, for this is a thing that depends on the intellect, which is the distinguishing feature of man — what sets him apart from every other living creature.

(4) The species of the contraries are five — for "contraries" is the broad name for all things opposed to each other, and each of these is one kind of them: opposites; privatives, or negatives; the distinguished; the conflicting; correlatives.

(5) The opposites are those in which one affirms and one denies the same thing. For example: walks, does not walk.
The rules of the opposites: 1. The opposites have no middle. Its explanation: for between denial and affirmation there is no middle. 2. When one of the opposites is laid down as true, the second is necessarily denied. 3. The predicate of a statement of opposites — one whose predicate is the denial of its subject — can never fit together with its subject. For example, let the statement be: A man is not a not-man; for man and not-man cannot join together in any way.
(6) The privatives are those that indicate a possession and its absence — a power that a thing has by its nature, and the lack of it; and they are divided into the complete and the incomplete.
(7) The complete are those that remove even the power to do the thing. For example: the blindness of one whose two eyes have been put out.

(8) The incomplete are those that remove the actuality of the possession, its working in practice, but the power remains in the subject. For example: sleep removes wakefulness in actuality, but the power remains, for him to wake in actuality.
The rules of absence: 1. The possession is better than the absence. 2. The possession and the absence revolve around one subject. 3. One to whom the possession belongs, the absence belongs; and one to whom the possession does not belong, the absence does not belong. For example: a man, to whom sight belongs, blindness belongs; a wall, to which sight does not belong, blindness does not belong — one does not call a wall blind. 4. When one of them is laid down, its fellow is necessarily denied.
(9) The distinguished are the different species that are under one genus — the different kinds within one broader class — or individuals under one species. What is one of them is not the other.
(10) The conflicting are those that conflict with each other in their quality or in their action. For example: heat and cold; the hot and the cold.

(11) The conflicting are divided into those with a middle and those without a middle. Those with a middle have a middle between them; those without a middle have no middle between them. For example: heat and cold have the lukewarm between them; but day and night have no middle between them.
The rules of the conflicting: 1. If one conflicting thing prevails entirely, it cancels its fellow entirely. For example: if heat prevails entirely, it cancels cold entirely. 2. The conflicting are both affirmations, and not denials. Its explanation: for if you say not hot, it does not conflict with not cold, since a thing can well be neither hot nor cold; but hot and cold together it cannot be. 3. The conflicting: their causes and their effects, their distinctive properties and their subjects, all of them conflict with each other as well.

(12) The correlatives are things in relation, in which one cannot be without its fellow; and they are contraries of each other. For example: the father is the contrary of the son, and the son is the contrary of the father — there is no father without a son, yet one man is not his own father and son.
The rules of the correlatives: 1. The knowledge of the correlatives is one, for neither is without its fellow; whoever knows one knows the other. 2. The correlatives, in respect of their being joined, are like a cause to each other. 3. When one is absent, its fellow is absent. 4. Of whatever the one is affirmed, its fellow is denied.

Testimony and the attested. The rules of testimony.
(1) Testimony and the attested is the affirming of a thing from outside it — the thing is established not by its own nature or causes, but by someone who bears witness to it; and it is divided into the Divine and the human.
(2) The Divine is when the words of Hashem, blessed be He, affirm it.

(3) The human is when a person affirms it; and it is divided into the many and the single. The many is when many testify to it; the single is when one testifies to it. The rules of testimony: As the witness, so the strength of the testimony. Its explanation: according to the standing of the witness and his importance, so is the strength of his testimony for our believing it.

The simple and the compound statement. The subject and the predicate. The link. The universal, the particular and the individual statement. The affirmative and the negative; the unconditional and the conditional. The restricting, the excepting and the qualifying. The true and the false. The necessary, the possible, the exact and the inexact.
(1) A statement is a joining of words in which one thing is affirmed of another thing, or one thing is denied of another thing. For example: The bread is white — it has affirmed whiteness of the bread; The bread is not black — it has denied blackness of it.
(2) The statement is divided into the simple and the compound.

(3) The simple is the statement that affirms or denies something. And there are four aspects to consider in it, and they are: the parts, the link, the species — what kind of statement it is — and the accidents, the qualities that a statement may or may not have, such as being true or false.
(4) The parts of statements are the subject and the predicate.
(5) The subject is that of which the affirmed thing is affirmed, or the denied thing is denied — what the statement is about.
(6) The predicate is what is affirmed or denied of the subject — what is said about it. For example: The bread is white. Bread is the subject; white is the predicate.

(7) The link is what links the predicate to the subject; and it can be stated, and it can be hidden. The stated is when the word hu — in Hebrew, the word that serves as "is" — or what indicates it, stands between the subject and the predicate; and the hidden is when the predicate is a verb. An example of the stated: The bread is white. An example of the hidden: Reuven ate — it is understood in it, Reuven did the act of eating. The link lies hidden inside the verb.
(8) The species: by it the statement is considered according to quantity and according to quality. According to quantity there will be three species of it: universal, particular and individual.

(9) The universal is that whose subject includes all that is of its sort, and the predicate is said of them all. For example: Every living creature has sensation: the subject includes everyone in whom there is the quality of life, and the predicate, that it has sensation, is said of them all.
(10) The particular is that whose subject includes some of what is of its sort, and of them the predicate is said. For example: Some living creatures speak.
(11) The individual is that whose subject is one individual. For example: Yerushalayim is a beautiful city.
(12) According to quality, the species of the statement will be two: affirmative or negative. The affirmative is one that affirms the predicate of the subject; the negative denies it of it.
(13) Statements as a whole are divided into two species: unconditional and conditional.

(14) The unconditional is one that affirms or denies without any condition; the conditional is one in which there is a condition along with the affirmation or the denial, something that sets a bound to it; and it is divided into a first and a second.

(15) The first conditional is one that has in it one of four things, and they are: necessity, impossibility, possibility, even balance — when either way is equally open. For example: necessity — fire must burn; impossibility — it is impossible for the part to be as the whole; possibility — a man may live long; even balance — a man is evenly balanced as to whether he will sit or not sit.

(16) The second conditional is divided into three species: the restricting conditional, the excepting conditional, the qualifying conditional.
The restricting is one that excludes from the subject or the predicate everything other than them. And it is done with the word only, or alone, and the like. The excepting is one that takes something out of the subject or out of the predicate; and this is with the word except, and the like. The qualifying is one that bounds the predicate in the subject to some respect; and it is done with the word according to, or in comparison with, or relative to, and the like.
An example of the restricting: Man alone speaks. The excepting: All silence is good, except from words of Torah. An example of the qualifying: Man is lowly in comparison with the angels.

(17) A statement can be true or false. The true is one that tells the thing as it is; the false, one that tells it as it is not. And in both of them it can be necessary or possible, exact or not exact.
(18) The necessary is one that is true and cannot be false, or false and cannot be true. For example, if you say, A living creature must have sensation.
(19) The possible is one that is true and can be false, or the reverse — false and can be true. For example: A man may live long.

(20) The exact is a statement that means by its words what they mean in grammar — their plain, literal sense; and the not exact is one that means by its words not what they mean in grammar. For example, if you say of some mighty man, This man is a lion, you do not understand an actual lion, but that his heart is like the heart of a lion (Shemuel II 17:10).

Simple, accidental and contrary conversion. The rules of conversion. Opposition; the conditions of opposition, its species and its rules.
(1) The changing of a statement is of two kinds: the one is conversion and the other is opposition. The conversion of a statement is putting the subject in the place of the predicate and the predicate in the place of the subject, and the statement remains true. And there are three species of it: simple, accidental and contrary.

(2) The simple is exchanging the subject with the predicate while the quantity and the quality are kept — the quantity being whether the statement speaks of all or of some, and the quality, whether it affirms or denies. Its explanation: it remains affirmative if it was affirmative, or negative if it was negative; and the same with the quantity. For example: Every man is a speaking living creature; every speaking living creature is a man.

(3) The accidental is one that keeps the quality but not the quantity. For example: Every speaking being is alive; some living being speaks. For the first is a universal statement, and the second a particular one.

(4) The contrary is one that keeps the quantity but not the quality. For example: Every speaking being is a living creature; everything that is not a living creature does not speak.
The rules of conversion: 1. The conversion of the universal affirmative is a particular affirmative and a universal negative. 2. The conversion of the particular affirmative is a particular affirmative. 3. The conversion of the universal negative is a universal negative. 4. The particular negative has no necessary conversion — none that must be true whenever it is true.
