For example: Every man is alive; and its conversions, some living being is a man; everything that is not alive is not a man. Some man is alive; some living being is a man. No man is a stone; no stone is a man. Some man is not wise — its conversion is not necessary, except the contrary one. One may not say "some wise being is not a man," but by the contrary conversion one may say, "something that is not wise is not a not-man."
(5) Opposition is a statement that is the opposite of a statement. Its explanation: that the one affirms and the other denies one thing of one subject.
(6) The aspects of opposition are two: the conditions and the species.

(7) The conditions of opposition are three: 1. The opposite statements must have the subjects of both, and their predicates, one and the same. For example: Man is a living creature; man is not a living creature. 2. They must be understood of one subject, in one respect, in one place, at one time. For example: Yitzchak had sons; Yitzchak had no sons — they are not opposites, for they are understood of two times: before his prayer and after his prayer (see Bereshit 25:21). And similarly: The seeds grow by means of the rain; the plants do not grow by means of the rain — they are understood — the first of the whole world, and the second of Egypt, where the fields are watered by the river and not by rain. 3. The opposites must be understood in a simple sense, without any sharing — no word in them may be a shared name, carrying two meanings. For example: Sartan is a living creature; sartan is not a living creature — the fish called sartan, the crab, is understood in the first, and the constellation, Cancer, which bears the same name, in the second.

(8) The species of opposites are two, and they are: complete opposition and incomplete. The complete is one in which, necessarily, one of them is false and one of them is true. And it is divided into two: a first and a second.

(9) The first is opposition between a universal and a particular, one affirmative and one negative; the second, between two individual statements. An example of the first: Every man is white; some man is not white. The second: Reuven is white; Reuven is not white.
The rules of complete opposition: Two complete opposites cannot be either both false or both true.
The incomplete is opposition between two universals. For example: Every man is righteous; no man is righteous.
The rules of the incomplete: Two incomplete opposites cannot be both true, and they can be both false — as here, when some men are righteous and some are not.

The conditional statement, the joining, the dividing, the separating and the relating.
(1) A compound statement is one whose content is compound — made up of two or more statements joined into one; and it divides into five kinds: conditional, joining, dividing, separating, relating.

(2) The parts of the conditional statement are two: the antecedent and the consequent; the part in which the condition is stated is the antecedent — the part that comes first; the second is the consequent — the part that follows from it.
For example, a conditional statement is: If you toil at your studies, you will certainly grow wise. If you toil at your studies is the antecedent; you will certainly grow wise is the consequent.

(3) The requirements of a condition are two: 1. That the whole of the affirming or the denying depends on the condition — the statement affirms or denies nothing outright, but only as resting on the condition.
For example, the statement we mentioned, If you toil and so on, does not affirm that you will toil at your studies, nor that you will certainly grow wise; rather, it lays down the consequent upon the laying down of the antecedent — once the first part is granted, the second is granted with it — that is: that if you toil at your studies, it will follow from this that you will certainly grow wise.
2. That it be true — and not on account of the parts by themselves, but on account of their conditional link, that the second really follows from the first.
For example, if you say, If man has two legs, he speaks, then the two parts, each one by itself, are true, but their link is false, for it does not follow from his having two legs that he will speak. And if you say, If the wall has eyes, it will certainly see, then the two parts are false, and your statement is true, for once it is laid down that it has eyes, it follows that it will see.

(4) The joined statement is one whose parts are joined by these links, in the words: while, then, not only, but also.
For example: Not only were we commanded concerning study, but also concerning deed.

(5) The affirming and the denying of the joined statement depend on the link, but its truth depends on each one of the parts.
Its explanation: for the statement we mentioned to be true, it must be true that we were commanded concerning study, and that we were commanded concerning deed as well; if either part is false, the whole statement is false.

(6) The dividing statement: its link is the word or; and its truth lies in the division being necessary — that one of its parts must be so.
For example: Now it is day or night.

(7) The separating statement is one that separates its content — it sets one part apart from, or against, the other; and its link is: not, but, although.
For example: Although we are in so long an exile, we hold fast to our Torah. The Torah is not servitude, but freedom.

(8) The relating statement is one whose parts are related to each other, and its links are: as … so, and the like.
For example: As the king, so the people; Where the gold is, there is the honor.

The syllogism and its power of producing. The complete syllogism. Major premise, minor, and conclusion. The incomplete, simple and compound. The conditional syllogism. The dividing.
(1) The syllogism is the putting together of two premises that have been established as true — a premise being a statement laid down first, from which something else is drawn — and producing from them a true conclusion.
Its explanation: the syllogism is the third action that the mind performs — after conceiving a thing and judging it in a statement — and it is reflecting to arrive at one thing out of another; that is, that out of an intelligible thing that has already been established and known it produces and brings forth anew another, which follows of necessity from the first.
Now the root of the syllogism is knowing what falls under a subject whose predicate you know — the subject being what a statement speaks about, and the predicate what it says of it — or what stands to it as a species to its genus — a narrower kind within a wider one — or what falls under the predicate of your subject; for whatever is included under your subject, you will necessarily judge that the predicate which applied to your subject applies to it; and if it is a species of it, then what applies to the genus will apply to every species of it. And so too with the predicate.
Its explanation: for whatever is included in the predicate which you know to be in your subject, you will decide that it is in it — in your subject — as well.
For example: you know that every man is a living creature. When you know that Reuven is included in "man," as a species under its genus, you will know that of necessity Reuven too is a living creature. And this is the foundation on which all syllogisms are built. Syllogisms do indeed have many ways of proceeding, but all of them return to this way, when you reflect on them.
For example, if you say: No man is an ox; some living creature is a man; therefore some living creature is not an ox.
Or if you say: Every speaking being is a man; no stone is a man; therefore no speaking being is a stone.
Or you say: Every speaking being is a body; no speaking being is a stone; therefore some body is not a stone.
You see that all of them return to the way I described. For when you know that no stone is a man, then of necessity no man is a stone; and then you say: Every speaking being is a man; it follows that it is not a stone — what is said of "man," that he is not a stone, is said of everything that falls under "man."
And so all the kinds of syllogisms — whether they are spelled out in all their parts or not spelled out, or are arranged in whatever order it may be — they all return to this way, and this is the whole of their power of producing a conclusion.
(2) The kinds of syllogisms are four: the complete syllogism, the incomplete, the conditional, and the dividing.

(3) The complete syllogism is one in which both of the producing premises and their conclusion are stated.
For example: Every man is living; Reuven is a man; therefore he is a living creature.

(4) The things to be distinguished in the complete syllogism are three: the known, the sought, and the comparing; and they called them major, minor, and conclusion — though not in that order: the known is the major premise, the comparing is the minor premise, and the sought is the conclusion, as the next paragraph shows.

(5) The known is the premise whose subject and predicate you know; the sought is the subject which you know and for which you seek to know a predicate; and the comparing is the premise in which you compare the sought subject with the known subject, so as to judge it, by this means, to have the known predicate.
For example: Every man is a living creature is the known, for you know its subject, which is "man," and its predicate, which is "living creature." Reuven is a living creature is the sought, for you know its subject, which is Reuven, and you sought to know its predicate — whether he is a living creature. And Reuven is a man is the comparing, for it compares your subject, which is Reuven, with the known subject, which is "man."
(6) The incomplete syllogism is one in which one of the producing premises is left unstated, and it is built of two statements only; and it divides into simple and compound.

(7) The simple is one that has two parts only. The first is called the antecedent, and the second the consequent.
For example: The branches of wisdom bring honor to man; therefore it is fitting that they be desired.
Or: What brings honor to man is fitting to be desired; therefore the branches of wisdom are fitting to be desired. And you will see that in the first example the first premise is left unstated — "what brings honor to man is fitting to be desired" — and in the second, the second — "the branches of wisdom bring honor to man."

(8) The compound divides into two. The first is one whose antecedent is made up of many subjects and one predicate; and some have called it "searching" — reasoning from many particular cases to a general rule.
For example: The wine of the land of France, the land of Italy, the land of Ashkenaz — Germany — the land of Sefarad — Spain — and the land of Togarmah — Turkey — warms; therefore all wine warms.

(9) The second compound is one whose antecedent is made up of many subjects and predicates taking each other's place one after another, step by step, so that the predicate of the one becomes the subject in the next.
For example: Every man is a living creature; every living creature has sensation; everything that has sensation is a living body; every living body is compound; therefore every man is compound.

(10) The conditional syllogism is one whose conclusion is set in the condition which is laid down in the first premise.
For example: If man is a living creature, he has sensation; but man is certainly a living creature; therefore he has sensation.

(11) The dividing syllogism is one whose first premise is divided by the word "or," and one of the parts is laid down and the other denied — one in the second premise and the other in the conclusion, in either order, as the two examples show.
For example: Now it is day or night; but it is not day; therefore it is night.
Or: Now it is day or night; but it is day; therefore it is not night.

The uses of the syllogism. The direct syllogism and the syllogism from the opposite.
(1) Until now we have explained the syllogisms themselves; now we shall explain the use of them.

(2) The syllogism serves for two things: the one, to bring forth a new intelligible thing — to come to know something one did not know before; the second, to uphold a thesis and prove it true — a thesis being a statement one has already put forward.
Its explanation: when there come to your mind the first two premises, your mind will of itself reflect, reason from them, and produce the conclusion, and then a new intelligible thing will come forth for you.
For example: when you have seen a shadow pass before you, it will at once become clear to you that a body passed there, for you will reason and say: There is no shadow except where there is a body; here a shadow passed; therefore here a body passed; and so in all similar cases. This is the first use of the syllogism.
But the second use is when you wish to prove true a statement that you make; then you will make use of the syllogism.
For example: suppose the statement was that a man's chief effort ought to be given to the Torah; when you wish to prove it true, you will use a syllogism such as this: A man's chief effort ought to be given to what is best for him. The Torah is what is best for man. Therefore a man's chief effort ought to be given to the Torah.

(3) The proving of a thesis will be either by a direct syllogism or by a syllogism from the opposite. The direct syllogism is a syllogism from whose premises there is produced the very conclusion we seek to prove.
The syllogism from the opposite is a syllogism built on the opposite of the thesis we seek to prove, from whose premises there is produced a conclusion that is manifestly false; and then we judge that our thesis is true — for if its opposite leads to a falsehood, the opposite must be false.
For example: suppose the statement was that the world was brought into being — that it had a beginning. To show that it is true, we say: If it were eternal — without beginning — the syllogism would come out in this way: Whatever is eternal cannot change; the world is eternal; therefore the world does not change. But this conclusion is manifestly false, for we see that the world changes; therefore it must be that the statement that the world is eternal is false, and that it was brought into being is true.

The refutations of the syllogism. The refutation of the conclusion on account of the order of the syllogism and on account of part of the syllogism. The refutation of a premise. Refutation in one respect. The deceptions of sharing and of mixing.
(1) Until now we have explained how a syllogism is put together; now we shall explain how it is refuted.
(2) A syllogism is refuted either entirely or in some respect.
(3) The refutation will be entire either in the conclusion or in one of the premises.
(4) The conclusion is refuted on account of the whole syllogism or on account of part of it.

(5) The conclusion is refuted on account of the whole syllogism if the order of the syllogism is not as it should be.
Its explanation: that the premises have no relation to the conclusion, or to one another.
For example: that there is mentioned in the conclusion what did not come in the known or in the comparing — in the major or the minor premise; that it gives the sought subject a predicate that is not the predicate of the known, or that it gives the predicate of the known to a subject that does not come under the subject of the known.
For example, that you say: Every man is a living creature; Reuven is a man; therefore he is not a living creature; or: therefore he begets children — a predicate the known premise never gave; or: therefore Shimon is a living creature — a subject the premises never spoke of.
Or that you say: Every man speaks; this bird speaks; therefore it is a man. Here the conclusion is refuted on account of the whole syllogism, for the predicate of the premise is not "man" but "speaks" — the conclusion gives the bird "man," which is the predicate of no premise; and "every man speaks" does not say that whatever speaks is a man.

(6) The conclusion is refuted on account of part of the syllogism if the predicate of one of the premises is not necessary — not bound to be so.
For example, that you say: A metal is either silver or gold; iron is a metal; therefore iron is either silver or gold. Here the predicate of the first premise is not necessary, for a thing can be a metal and be neither silver nor gold.

(7) The refutation of a premise will be if the premise is false; that is, if it affirms of a subject a predicate that ought to be denied of it, or denies what ought to be affirmed, according to the rules of the logical descriptions that were explained above — what may truly be said of a thing, as the earlier chapters set out.

(8) Refutation in one respect is if there is said in the premise, as a general rule, what is so only in a certain relation and in one respect, for then we grant it in one respect and deny it in another respect; and this may be in the subject or in the predicate.
For example: Every man begets children; this child is a man; therefore he begets children. We will refute the one premise in part, and say: Every man who is grown and not barren begets children, but not every man without qualification; therefore it is not necessary that this child will beget children. And this is the distinction in the subject — the premise held only for some men, not for every man.
Or that you say: Man speaks; the mute is a man; therefore the mute speaks. The one premise will be refuted in part, and we will say: Every man who has nothing preventing his speech speaks, but the man who has something preventing his speech does not speak.

(9) All syllogisms, for them to be true, must be cleansed of deceptions — faults of reasoning that make a false conclusion look sound; and these are of two kinds: the first, sharing; the second, mixing.

(10) Sharing is the sharing of words in their meaning — one word that carries several meanings — so that at times, according to one meaning, a certain predicate suits them, and according to another meaning, it does not. And if the premise comes first in one of the meanings and the conclusion is in the other meaning, this is a deception.

(11) Mixing is when one does not examine the predicate as to what relation it has to its subject: whether essential or accidental — whether it belongs to what the thing is, or only happens to be in it; whether in potential or in actuality, and the like.
The sum of the matter: the conclusion must resemble its premises with an essential and complete resemblance. And if it resembles them only in part, and differs from them in its essential truth, this is a deception.
For example, if you say: Man speaks; So-and-so, who is silent, is a man; therefore So-and-so, who is silent, speaks; this is a deception, for man speaks in potential, but not always in actuality.

General order. The intellectual and the practical. The particular. Discovery. The discovery of theses. The discovery of proofs. The examination of a thesis. The imagined debate. The bodily debate. The subject of the debate and the manner of the debate. The debaters and their task. Deflection and refutation. The primary and the secondary purpose. Examination.
(1) Until now we have explained the syllogism. Now we shall explain order, which is that by which the parts of a study are arranged properly, according to their rank, and it is divided into general and particular order.
Its explanation: order is a straight road, so that one who walks on it will reach his goal correctly, without turning aside from it.

(2) General order is the order of one of the studies as a whole, which by specific laws guides a person to the knowledge of one of the branches of wisdom, or of the crafts, as he proceeds from the matters that come first and are better known to those that come later and are more hidden.
Its explanation: the things that come first and are better known are the general ones. For example, the genera are better known than the species and come before them — one knows that a thing is a living creature before one knows which kind of creature it is — and likewise the simple things are prior to the compound ones. Accordingly, in an orderly study the study of the general things must come before the study of the particulars, and that of the simple things before that of the compound ones.
For example, in grammar one must first speak of the letters, after that of the words and the vowel points, after that of the parts of speech — the nouns, the verbs and the particles — the small joining words — and after that of the joining of statements — how words are put together into sentences.

(3) Further, general order is divided into intellectual and practical. The intellectual is when the parts of one of the intellectual studies — the sciences that seek only to know — are arranged in such a way that from knowledge of the subject of that study we go on to knowledge of its causes, and from them to the considerations of the genus, and from them to those of the species — first what is true of the whole kind, then what is true of each species within it.
For example, in natural science, first the definition of body is explained, since body is the concern of that science — the thing it studies; after that the inner causes and the outer ones are explained — the matter and form within the body, and the maker and purpose outside it; after that all the species are explained, that is, the simple ones — the elements of fire, air, water and earth — first, and after that one goes on to the compound ones according to their ranks.

(4) The practical is when the parts of one of the studies of a craft — a study that seeks to make or do something — are arranged in this way: that from knowledge of the purpose we come to knowledge of the means needed to attain it.
For example, in logic the purpose is explained first, which is to discern things as they truly are; after that the means that lead to this are explained, that is, the logical descriptions — the terms of logic set out in the earlier chapters — the statements, and the syllogisms, and order. This is the order of this very book.
(5) Particular order is that which guides a person to the knowledge of some one intelligible matter in particular, not of a whole branch of wisdom, and it is divided into discovery and examination.
(6) Discovery is the discovery of theses — claims about a matter — and of syllogisms to prove them, whose laws were explained above.

(7) The discovery of theses is to examine, in some subject, one of the twenty-one considerations that were explained above — the twenty-one names that serve logic, listed in chapter 4: cause and effect, subject and the attached, whole and part, and the rest.
Its explanation: we have already explained above how these twenty-one considerations are the sum of all that can be affirmed or denied of any subject whatever, and from this the theses are built, for they are nothing but the affirming or denying of something of the subject. However, the order that is usually kept in investigating these considerations in any subject whatever, as far as they apply to it, is this:
1. The name: whether it is a name of one meaning, or shared, or borrowed, and the like among the other kinds of name. And this should be understood first, so that we not be in doubt about the subject we are dealing with — whether the word means one thing or several.
2. The genus: here it is examined under which genus of the ten first genera it enters — substance, quantity, quality and the other highest headings of all that exists — for as the genus changes, its laws change, as is explained in the rules of the ten genera that we mentioned.
3. All the causes. 4. The most notable effects. 5. The attached — the things joined to a subject — those proper to it alone, those shared with others, the preceding and the following — those that come before it and those that follow it — and all the rest. 6. The definition. 7. The division into building parts, if the subject is a built whole — a whole built of parts, as a house of its walls and roof. 8. The division into species, if the subject is a genus. 9. The things compared with it, those equal to it and those like it, in all their parts. 10. The things that differ from it and the contraries, in all their parts; for knowing them, too, helps greatly to clarify the knowledge of the subject.

(8) The discovery of syllogisms is the discovery of proofs to establish the truth of theses, or to disprove them; and its source is the twenty-one considerations that we explained.
Its explanation: for there is no syllogism in the world that shows the truth of a thesis, or its falsehood, that is not born of one of these considerations.
For example, if the thesis is that it is fitting to give the Torah great honor, you will prove the truth of the thesis by a syllogism such as this: "Whatever is related to the Creator, blessed be He, it is fitting to give great honor; — this is the major premise — the Torah is related to the Creator, blessed be He; — the minor premise — if so, it is fitting to give it great honor" — the conclusion. Now, this syllogism is born of the attached, which I explained in their place (chapter 9). For one of the things attached to the Torah is its being divine, meaning, related to the Creator, blessed be He. And so you are to judge with all syllogisms.

(9) The examination of a thesis, to confirm it or to disprove it, is done either by itself or in a debate. "By itself" is when we examine a thesis on our own, without an opponent, by means of the fitting considerations.
Its explanation: by means of the twenty-one considerations that we mentioned above, from which we draw all the syllogisms. Now, when you wish to examine a thesis, you will need to look first at its two parts, that is, the subject and the predicate, and to remove from them every doubt of shared meaning — any word that could mean more than one thing — until they are known to you as they truly are; after that, the quantity of the thesis: whether it is universal, particular or individual; after that you are to look at the essence of the thesis, that is, whether it is affirmative or negative, whether it is necessary or possible; after that you are to consider whether it is true or false, that is, whether it agrees with the rules that we set out beforehand in the twenty-one considerations, or whether it contradicts them, or whether it follows from them of necessity: if it follows from them of necessity, it is necessarily true; if it contradicts them, it is false; if it agrees with them but is not compelled by them, it is possible.

(10) "In a debate" is when two different or contrary theses are stated, and we draw up battle between them by means of syllogisms that support the one or the other, and the effort is to refute the misleading syllogisms and to uphold the true ones, until the true thesis is established; and this is done either in an imagined debate or in a bodily debate.

(11) The imagined debate is when one man does the work of the second as well, playing both sides himself: that is, he states his thesis as true, and afterward raises objections against it with syllogisms that would show it false, after that he refutes those syllogisms, and upholds his thesis and shows its truth.

(12) The bodily debate is one that takes place between two actual bodies — two real people — one proposing a thesis and one objecting to it. And in this, four considerations are examined: the first, the subject; the second, the manner; the third, the debaters; the fourth, the purpose.

(13) The subject is the matter, or thesis, about which the questioner and the respondent carry on their give-and-take. The give-and-take of debate ought to be only about a matter whose truth is not plain to all, for about things plain to all it is merely superfluous; and about a matter that it is possible to know, for about things impossible to grasp, give-and-take is futile, superfluous and unfitting; and it should be a matter whose knowledge is of benefit to some branch of wisdom or some craft, for if not, it is nothing but idle talk.

(14) The manner is that the give-and-take be clear, without deceptions — arguments that only seem sound; that it be with composure and calm, without haste and anger; that it be in a brief and logical way.
Its explanation: for if the objections and the answers are not set out in a logical way, so that the subjects and the predicates are examined, the affirmations and the negations, and all the other conditions of statements, then the falsehood and the error will not come to light, and its place will not be known, and it will slip past the mind without its noticing it; which is not so when all the definitions are examined as they should be, for then whatever is unfitting is revealed at once — whatever does not keep the law of proper relation in theses — between a subject and what is said of it.
However, a great many words as well, even if they are proper, weary the mind, and it grows tired of them, and it cannot examine them with the precision that is needed; for their burden upon it becomes too great, and it does not have the strength to distinguish between them and to understand their fine details; and so it turns out affirming what ought to be denied, or the reverse, without knowing it.
(15) The debaters are: the one, the proposer, who is himself the respondent, and the second, the questioner who objects to him.
(16) The proposer must explain his thesis well, in a brief way, and not at greater length than is enough, and he should assert as affirmed only what is made necessary for him by a true syllogism.
(17) The task of the questioner lies in what comes before he objects, at the time he objects, and after he objects.

(18) Before he objects: to listen well to the proposal of the proposer in all its parts, so as to understand it properly; after that, to examine them closely, whether there is reason to oppose one of them, whether by deflection or by refutation.

(19) "By deflection" — pushing the thesis aside without disproving it — is when necessity is lacking in the proposer's thesis — nothing compels us to accept it — even if the questioner does not show it false.
(20) "By refutation" is when his thesis is false, by force of a strong syllogism that refutes it.

(21) At the time he objects: he is to set out his objection in a brief and logical way, according to what it is, whether a deflection or a refutation.
Its explanation: for a refutation is not like a deflection. For a refutation must have the force of a decisive, strong syllogism, like the proposal itself; but as for a deflection — as long as there is no proof that compels the truth of the thesis, we may decline to accept it, pushing it aside with a deflection alone.
(22) After he objects: to listen well to the proposer as he answers his objection, and to acknowledge the truth.

(23) The task of the respondent lies before he answers and at the time he answers. Before he answers: to listen well to the objection and to discern its substance: whether it truly opposes his proposal or not, whether its construction is logical or not, whether its premises and its conclusion are necessary or not.
Its explanation: for if its substance does not really oppose his proposal, its refutation does not touch him, and he need not trouble himself with it, so as not to stray from his subject; if its construction is not logical, he is to show the questioner the place of the error, and tell him to set out his objection properly; if its premises or its conclusion are not necessary, he is to refute them; and if the objection is true, he is to acknowledge the truth and withdraw from his proposal. What he does in each of these cases is his task at the time he answers.
(24) The purpose of a debate is divided into primary and secondary.
(25) The primary is the grasping of the truth; the secondary, the sharpening of the mind.

(26) Until now we have explained discovery. Now we shall explain examination, which is to examine the parts of the statements and to set them in their logical ranks.
Its explanation: for after we know what to deny or affirm of one of the subjects, and the syllogisms that prove the truth of one of the theses, from this we build discourses and accounts in fine language, as is fitting, and arrange the matters with fullness of speech and the other ornaments of eloquence that are made to sweeten the words. But to test the discourses, we shall need to dissect them, and to separate the matters of fine language and the ways of telling on their own, and the logical parts on their own, stripped and bare of all the other matters of the telling, and the syllogisms in their form and their order; and then we shall be able to judge them and to test them. Now, the making of this dissection is the examination that we mentioned. The order of carrying out this examination, then, is this: first of all, you must read, and read again, and a third time the discourse or the account that you wish to dissect, and consider it well until you recognize its subject: whether it is one or more, whether it is simple or composite. For if you do not recognize all this clearly, you will stray far from the way of that account and of that discourse.
And after you have recognized the subject, or the subjects, that are in the account, then you are to separate out the points, or the proofs, contained in it, and distinguish between those most essential to the subject and those not so essential. And if the subjects are many, you are to set each subject apart by itself, with its points and its proofs, so as not to mix one subject with another, nor the conditions of one subject with the conditions of another. After that you are to set out the proofs in their divisions, in their order and form, and discern the proofs that establish the truth of the subjects and those that add explanation and broaden the main subject; and so all the parts will be found set out before you, so that you can consider them as is fitting and recognize the truth as it truly is, with the help of Heaven.
Finished and complete; praise to Hashem, Creator of the world.
